sources.title: MoMA — “Good Design” collection term
sources.supports: Concise institutional account of MoMA’s late-1930s–1950s Good Design initiatives, affordability, usefulness, and everyday objects.

sources.title: MoMA — *What Was Good Design? MoMA’s Message, 1944–56*
sources.supports: Shows that “Good Design” was promoted and disputed, and was broader than a small set of furniture icons.

sources.title: MoMA — *The Value of Good Design*
sources.supports: Strong source on democratizing claims, Cold War reconstruction, global examples, and the need to reassess those values today.

sources.title: MoMA press archive — *Organic Design in Home Furnishings*
sources.supports: Primary institutional documentation for the 1940–41 competition and the Eames/Saarinen molded-plywood origin story.

sources.title: Library of Congress — Eames exhibition, “Science”
sources.supports: First-party exhibition evidence for the Eameses’ systems thinking, Case Study House 8, trade-catalog components, exhibitions, and science communication.

sources.title: Library of Congress HABS — Eames House documentation
sources.supports: Measured historical documentation and bibliography for Case Study House 8; useful against simplified lifestyle retellings.

sources.title: Getty Conservation Institute — Eames House Conservation Project
sources.supports: Conservation-led account of the house as architecture, working environment, collection, landscape, and lived interior.

sources.title: Getty Conservation Institute — Eames House Conservation Management Plan
sources.supports: Deep, citable primary research on design development, materials, significance, alterations, and conservation policy.

sources.title: Charles & Ray Eames Foundation — Molded Plywood Group
sources.supports: Designer-foundation account of compound-curved plywood, wartime experimentation, mass production, and the 1946 MoMA show.

sources.title: Charles & Ray Eames Foundation — Children’s Plywood Chair
sources.supports: Useful counterexample to luxury-icon framing: lightweight, stackable, child-scaled, production- and distribution-aware design.

sources.title: Herman Miller — Eames Molded Plywood design story
sources.supports: Licensed manufacturer history for material trials, production, and iterative design. Cross-check promotional language against museum sources.

sources.title: Vitra Design Museum — Online Collection
sources.supports: Searchable museum collection and archives, including Charles and Ray Eames and Alexander Girard; good object-level follow-up source.

sources.title: Knoll — Florence Knoll
sources.supports: Manufacturer archive on the Planning Unit, space planning, corporate interiors, collaboration, and Florence Knoll’s own furniture.

sources.title: Knoll — Harry Bertoia
sources.supports: Manufacturer archive on Cranbrook, plywood work with Eames, wire experiments, sculpture, and the 1952 furniture collection.

sources.title: Knoll — designer archive index
sources.supports: Useful map of the broader Knoll network: Florence Knoll, Saarinen, Bertoia, Risom, Noguchi, Reich, Mies, and others.

sources.title: Cooper Hewitt — “Material Masters”
sources.supports: Museum account linking Cranbrook experiments, molded veneer, wartime materials, and postwar mass manufacture.

sources.title: Cooper Hewitt — “The ES 108 Sofa”
sources.supports: Object-focused account of Eames/Herman Miller production and modern commercial/domestic interiors.

sources.title: Newfields — Miller House and Garden
sources.supports: Authoritative house-museum source for Saarinen architecture, Girard interiors, Kiley landscape, and total-environment collaboration.

sources.title: Newfields Archives — Miller House and Garden Collection, 1953–2009, undated
sources.supports: Current primary collection guide with dates, designers, project records, and preservation context.

sources.title: Architectural Digest (2023) — “Midcentury-Modern Architecture: Everything You Should Know”
sources.supports: Expert-assisted contemporary definition; distinguishes a design program from “anything made mid-century” and identifies architecture/material principles.

sources.title: Architectural Digest — “17 Midcentury-Modern Living Rooms”
sources.supports: Evidence of current warm, moody, layered usage: dark woods, natural materials, oversized low seating, vintage plus contemporary art.

sources.title: House & Garden (2025) — “What is it about mid-century design classics?”
sources.supports: Current practitioner discussion of longevity, mixability, human scale, repair/investment value, and new “future heirlooms.”

sources.title: Livingetc (2025) — “Mid-Century Modern Living Room … ‘Collected’ Look”
sources.supports: Clear example of the current “collected,” warm-wood, leather, glass, metal, open-plan interpretation. Commercial; use as usage evidence only.

sources.title: Wallpaper* (2025) — Charles and Ray Eames furniture guide
sources.supports: Recent high-quality synthesis connecting wartime plywood, affordable LCW, office furniture, licensed production, films, play, and systems thinking.

sources.title: Wallpaper* (2025) — Eames House, Pacific Palisades
sources.supports: Current house-museum/conservation context and a lived-in, layered Eames interior—useful against sterile “MCM showroom” styling.

sources.title: Kristina Wilson — *Mid-Century Modernism and the American Body*
sources.supports: Essential monograph on how race, gender, identity, advice literature, marketing, and bodily norms shaped postwar modern design.

sources.title: Kristina Wilson (2015) — “Like a ‘Girl in a Bikini Suit’ … Herman Miller”
sources.supports: Peer-reviewed object/marketing analysis; cautions that supposedly neutral abstract furniture was framed by racialized and gendered narratives.

sources.title: CAA Reviews — review of *Mid-Century Modernism and the American Body*
sources.supports: Scholarly assessment and useful synopsis of white masculinity, *Ebony* counter-narratives, bodily control, and non-Western objects in staged interiors.

sources.title: Docomomo US (2025) — “Black Modernist Architects and Designers”
sources.supports: Direct corrective to a white-male canon; broadens the atlas’s people and project pool rather than treating diversity as an aside.

sources.title: Parsons/Cooper Hewitt History of Design — review of Wilson
sources.publisher: Parsons / Cooper Hewitt History of Design
sources.supports: Accessible teaching-oriented explanation of why the Jim Crow, civil-rights, class, and gender context belongs inside—not outside—the design story.
